tier_reason: Upgraded from C: the EuroSys 2025 Eg-walker paper (Gentle and Kleppmann) benchmarks diamond-types against Automerge and Yjs with public artifact code in josephg/egwalker-paper (step2b-benchmarks.sh; DT bench crate merge_norm, tools/paper-benchmarks/src/main.rs for Automerge and Yrs, tools/bench-yjs/bench-remote.js for Yjs; means in results/timings.json), and the paper footnote states Ryzen 7950x, rustc 1.78.0 release with -C target-cpu=native, Node.js v22.2.0. The A tier covers the native Rust library only; nothing measures the wasm npm builds.

corrections.baseline: Automerge v0.5.9 (Rust) and Yjs v13.6.10 (JavaScript on Node.js v22.2.0), per the EuroSys 2025 Eg-walker paper; also the authors' own reference CRDT (Yrs, the Rust port of Yjs, was run but omitted from the paper)
corrections.claimed_speedup: Native Rust, CPU time to merge a whole editing trace received from a remote replica, means from egwalker-paper results/timings.json (derived from page data): diamond-types 1.77-82.6 ms vs Automerge 485-24,636 ms, i.e. 22x (A2) to 404x (S3); vs Yjs (55-88 ms) 32.5x on S1, 31.8x on S2, 22.3x on S3, 1.5x on C1, 10.0x on A1, 3.2x on A2, but 0.67x on C2 (diamond-types slower, 82.6 vs 55.2 ms). Cached document reload takes 0.012-0.12 ms against CRDT load times equal to their merge times. Paper text: 160,000x faster than OT on trace A2 and 7-10x faster than the authors' reference CRDT on the sequential traces. The README's link to a '5000x faster' blog post and its 'another 10-80x' claim, and the About text 'The world's fastest CRDT', could not be checked (blog unreachable).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.78.0 in release mode with -C target-cpu=native, Rust benchmarks pinned to one core (taskset 0x1 nice -10), Criterion.rs; Yjs on Node.js v22.2.0 via smolbench (paper footnote). The artifact README says the current results used Rust 1.80 and Node.js v21, so the two sources disagree on versions.
corrections.workload: Merging each of seven real editing traces (S1-S3 sequential, C1-C2 concurrent, A1-A2 asynchronous) into an empty document as if received from a remote replica, plus reloading the saved document; Yjs is timed on Y.applyUpdateV2 of the pre-encoded document, Automerge and Yrs on loading their encoded documents.
corrections.caveats: All measured numbers are for the native Rust library; no benchmark of the wasm builds exists, and the npm packages diamond-types-node and diamond-types-web were last published as 1.0.2 on 2023-05-15 (crates.io 1.0.0 on 2022-08-25; the README says the published crate is quite out of date), so the wasm packages predate the benchmarked May-2024 code. Mixed against Yjs: diamond-types is slower on C2 (82.6 vs 55.2 ms) and only 1.5x faster on C1, although the paper text says it is significantly faster than Yjs on C1, C2 and A2. Yrs was omitted from the paper on the grounds that it was slower than Yjs, yet the artifact's committed results/timings.json shows Yrs at 8-13 ms, faster than diamond-types on C1 (4.8x), C2 (9.5x) and A2 (1.8x); Yjs and Yrs times are nearly flat across traces of very different size, which an enricher should check. Diamond-types is also slightly slower than the authors' reference CRDT on C1 and C2. The cached-load advantage comes from storing the final document text, a design difference rather than a like-for-like load. Automerge was measured as its Rust v0.5.9 core, not the JavaScript build. The paper is first-party (diamond-types' author, co-authored with Automerge's creator) but peer-reviewed. The 5000x and 10-80x README figures remain unverified because josephg.com did not resolve. Not part of dmonad/crdt-benchmarks (its README lists Yjs, ywasm, Loro and Automerge only).

notes: Upgraded C to A on the EuroSys 2025 Eg-walker paper artifact (josephg/egwalker-paper), which is reproducible with code, compiler, flags and CPU model, but it measures native Rust only; consider a category override out of wasm-libraries-and-apps or a caveat that the wasm packages (npm 1.0.2, 2023) are unmeasured. Shortcomings to record: slower than Yjs on C2 and than Yrs on C1, C2 and A2 in the artifact's own results; Yrs omitted from the paper; README 5000x claim unverifiable (blog josephg.com unreachable, getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND). Metadata checked: ISC, 1.8k stars, last commit 2026-09-02, not archived.

tier_reason: First-party README table produced by public benchmark code (bench/index.js run by `chomp bench`) with compilers and flags in chompfile.toml, but the machine is only 'a standard desktop machine' with no CPU model; the Acorn comparison is a prose claim with no benchmark code.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README Package Exports table (3.1 MB test/samples set, Node.js 26, chomp bench): full Wasm build 4.7 ms/MB cold and 3.2 ms/MB warm versus the CSP asm.js build of the same C lexer at 14.9 / 6.3 ms/MB (3.2x cold, 2.0x warm, derived from page data); minimal Wasm build 4.5 / 3.1 versus minimal asm.js 10.8 / 5.7 ms/MB (2.4x cold, 1.8x warm, derived from page data). README prose: 'Angular 1 (720KiB) is fully parsed in 1ms, in comparison to the fastest JS parser, Acorn which takes over 100ms' (no Acorn row or benchmark code).
corrections.caveats: First-party numbers on an unnamed machine, one run per build. bench/index.js times only the four package builds (no Acorn or any independently written JS lexer); cold time excludes module load and init. The >100x comparison against Acorn compares a module-syntax lexer with a full AST parser and is not backed by any table or code. The asm.js baseline is the same C source compiled by the 2020-era fastcomp emscripten 1.40.1 (-Oz --closure 1), so the ratio measures Wasm versus asm.js output of one lexer, not Wasm versus a JS implementation. The Wasm builds use -Oz (size) rather than -O3; the full build needs Wasm SIMD (-DLEXER_SIMD) while the minimal build targets MVP. A listed entry, fast-es-module-lexer (paper:r1ck404-fast-packages-fast-es-module-lexer, tier A), reports 6.6-18x faster scans than es-module-lexer 1.7.0, so es-module-lexer is no longer the fastest option for this task (the current 3.0.3 full build is compiled with -DLEXER_SIMD; whether 1.7.0 used SIMD was not checked).

notes: Record accurate; table numbers and derived ratios match the README, flags match chompfile.toml (emcc 6.0.0, fastcomp 1.40.1). Shortcomings to record: baseline is its own asm.js build, Acorn >100x claim is prose only, no CPU model, and the listed fast-es-module-lexer beats it 6.6-18x. Metadata checked: MIT, 1.0k stars, last commit 2026-10-06 (v3.0.3 released 2026-10-05).

tier_reason: First-party README ratios plus one screenshot from the repo's example app (example/test-fast-md5/src/App.vue, public); no hardware, browser, file set or run count, and the 8x single-thread figure has no data at all.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: '~8x faster than spark-md5' in single-thread mode and '~16x faster' with multi-thread workers ('in specific scenarios'). The only data is a screenshot of the example app (docs/a3d25c4789a9937d8a1fc76c12b61152.png): 174 files, 100.0% hash match, SparkMD5 total 109,271.50 ms vs Fast-MD5-Web worker pool 6,329.50 ms, labelled a 1626.4% improvement (17.3x, derived from page data). No measurement is shown for the 8x single-thread claim. README also: a 10 MB file with 4 workers takes ~151 ms with SharedArrayBuffer vs ~200 ms without (~25% faster).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: RustCrypto md-5 0.10.6 via wasm-bindgen, [profile.release] opt-level = "s" (wasm/Cargo.toml); Rust, wasm-bindgen and browser versions for the screenshot run unstated
corrections.workload: Browser MD5 of a user-selected set of 174 files (sizes unstated, not in the repo) in the example Vue app: SparkMD5 on the main thread reading 2 MB FileReader chunks for all files under Promise.all, then fast-md5-web's Md5CalculatorPool with navigator.hardwareConcurrency workers; hashes cross-checked.
corrections.caveats: Screenshot only: no hardware, browser, core count, file sizes or repetition; the 174 input files are not in the repo (example/test-fast-md5/public/test-files holds small fixtures). The harness compares a worker pool sized to navigator.hardwareConcurrency against single-threaded SparkMD5 on the main thread, so the 16-17x is mostly parallelism, not per-core speed; SparkMD5 always runs first, so the second run may benefit from warm file caches. The 8x single-thread claim has no published measurement. The MD5 core is the RustCrypto md-5 crate built with opt-level 's' (size); the project is a wasm-bindgen and worker-pool wrapper around it. The listed hash-wasm (wave 13) also benchmarks MD5 against spark-md5 and was not compared here. The README calls it 'possibly the fastest'.

notes: Record accurate in substance; added the screenshot's numbers (17.3x for the worker pool, derived) and the harness flaws. Shortcomings to record: multi-thread pool versus single-thread spark-md5, fixed run order, undisclosed hardware/browser/files, 8x single-thread claim unmeasured, thin wrapper over RustCrypto md-5. Metadata checked: MIT, 98 stars, last commit 2026-03-15, not archived, not a fork.
